systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.
Source : Verfassungsblog
Rubrique : Droit
Date du flux : 17/11/2026
Auteur : Esmeralda Colombo; Siri Gloppen; Yann Robiou du Pont
Titre d'origine : The Great Norwegian Reset

ARTICLE :
On 13 November 2026, the Norwegian Supreme Court, sitting as an eleven-judge Grand Chamber, delivered a landmark judgment in the North Sea Fields case. The Court held that environmental impact assessments (EIAs) must address downstream emissions from burning extracted oil and gas (Scope 3). By a 6–5 majority, it also required the emissions of Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil to be assessed alongside those of other existing and approved petroleum projects on the Norwegian continental shelf. Finding that the Ministry of Energy had failed to meet this requirement, even in its subsequent assessments, the Court declared the development approvals invalid (HR-2026-2428-S, paras 225, 234, 244), short of ordering operations to stop. The decision’s constitutional significance lies in the role of procedural environmental rights, which ultimately require thorough and independent assessments, as well as the inclusive participation of the public in how the State assesses climate harm.
Greenpeace Nordic and Natur og Ungdom (Nature and Youth) brought the proceedings against the Norwegian State. Save the Children Norway intervened through written submissions on children’s rights. The Norwegian Association of Local and Regional Authorities and the Norwegian National Human Rights Institution also submitted observations.
The three developments hold an estimated 875 million barrels of oil equivalent. Yet, the ruling matters beyond this scale: it challenges the assessment of petroleum projects in isolation.
The Road to the Supreme Court
In June 2023, the environmental organisations challenged the approvals of the three Plans for Development and Operation (PDOs), arguing that the EIAs had omitted emissions from the eventual combustion of the oil and gas. They also sought interim relief.
In January 2024, the Oslo District Court declared the approvals invalid and granted interim relief. In the appeals brought by the State, the Borgarting Court of Appeal suspended the injunction and sought an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court, which held in May 2025 that the EIA Directive required downstream combustion emissions to be assessed (Case E-18/24).
Meanwhile, the operators submitted supplementary environmental reports, followed by public consultations. In August and December 2024, the Ministry decided not to revoke the approvals. In November 2025, the Court of Appeal declared those decisions invalid: although it considered the supplementary reports sufficient, the Ministry’s own assessment was deemed deficient, and the State appealed.
While the appeal was pending, the government in May 2026 issued a Royal Decree declining to revoke the approvals, but the appeal decided by the Supreme Court concerned only the Ministry’s 2024 decisions.
This Norwegian case has already travelled. The Oslo District Court judgment was cited by the UK Supreme Court in Finch v Surrey County Council ([2024] UKSC 20, paras 169–172). Finch, in turn, was later relied upon by the Scottish Court of Session in quashing the Jackdaw and Rosebank consents (Greenpeace Ltd v Advocate General for Scotland, [2025] CSOH 10). Meanwhile, in Norway, the Borgarting Court of Appeal referred questions concerning downstream emissions to the EFTA Court (Case E-18/24), whose advisory opinion was cited by Judges Bhandari and Cleveland in their joint declaration attached to the ICJ’s Advisory Opinion on Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change (Joint declaration, para 16 with reference to Case E-18/24, para 17), as well as by the Danish Energy Board of Appeals, which required reconsideration for the approval of the Hejre oil field.
The Supreme Court’s Decision
At first glance, the judgment turns on whether Article 3(1) of the EU EIA Directive (2011/92/EU) encompasses downstream combustion emissions among a project’s significant direct and indirect effects. But its reasoning reaches further, engaging with causation, cumulative harm and the constitutional value of environmental procedure, and is historic in both breadth and depth.
In breadth, the majority, led by Justice Poulsen, situated the Directive within a wider legal landscape. It referred to the ICJ’s view that customary international law requires States to exercise due diligence to prevent significant climate harm and to consider cumulative effects of activities under their jurisdiction or control (paras 177). The Court also drew on the ECtHR’s Greenpeace Nordic v Norway, under which authorities must consider whether petroleum developments are compatible with national and international obligations to protect against climate harm (paras 184–191).
In depth, the decision is anchored in consequential reasoning. Once extracted, oil and gas will almost inevitably be burned, generating emissions unless carbon capture intervenes (paras 149–150). This reasoning can be called the logical inseparability of extraction and combustion, and it reflects IPCC science, whose findings Norway had already recognised, alongside its domestic and international climate commitments (paras 99–107, 151).
According to the Court, the EIA Directive’s requirement that gross combustion emissions be not only described, but also assessed in an EIA before approval of a PDO is consistent with the wording of Norway’s Petroleum Act and the Petroleum Regulations, and could be gleaned already from the first climate case against the Norwegian state, Peoples v Arctic Oil, which was decided in 2020, whereby “global climate effects” are to be subject to an EIA in connection with an application for PDO approval (HR-2020-2472-P, paras 212, 214, 216, 218 and 241 as cited in para 155).
Further, the court held that neither the EIA Directive nor international and regional law impose a more extensive obligation to carry out an EIA in proceedings concerning PDO approval that also considers the global climate budget or consequential effects. On the global carbon budget, the court referred to the Paris Agreement Article 4 (as referenced in para 189) and Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) on the obligation to carry out “adequate, timely and comprehensive” EIAs (People v Arctic Oil, para 318, as quoted in para 184).   Similarly, when describing the project’s “direct effects and any indirect, secondary and cumulative effects”, the EIA Directive does not impose the carbon budget approach as account should, rather than shall, be taken of “the environmental protection objectives established at Union or Member State level which are relevant to the project”(point 5, para 2, of Annex IV to the EIA Directive, as referenced in paras 181 and 182). In contrast, the Court of Appeal had held that assessments were to be carried out in light of the remaining global carbon budgets, that is, the maximum amount of CO₂ that can be released into the atmosphere before the temperature rises to a given level (para 179).
On consequential effects, the Norwegian Supreme Court stated that there is no doubt that an EIA must cover the project’s effects on all the factors listed in Article 3(1) of the EIA Directive, namely human beings, human health, biodiversity, land, soil, water, air, climate, material assets, cultural heritage and landscape, as well as the interactions between these factors (para 194). The Court clarified, however, that the question at issue was a different one: whether the assessment must also encompass the consequential effects that the project’s impacts on one or more of these factors may have on other factors, and answered in the negative (paras 196ff).
The Norwegian Continental Shelf, and Its Dissent
The disagreement between the majority and minority judges concerned cumulative assessment. The majority holds that the EIA Directive requires an impact assessment to describe and assess the combustion emissions both of the project at hand and, cumulatively, of other existing and approved projects on the Norwegian shelf, together with their effect on global temperature rise (paras 178 and 214ff). The State argued that cumulation matters only to prevent “salami-slicing”, that is, splitting a project to dodge the assessment threshold. The majority rejected this: cumulation governs not only whether an assessment is triggered, but also what it must contain (paras 164–165). Two limits frame this duty: the continental shelf, because Norway can license petroleum nowhere else (para 167) and the petroleum sector, since adding every other sector would make the assessment disproportionately burdensome (para 168). The majority also stressed that the duty can be easily fulfilled by reference to reserve data for every field, which is public, and simple computations on gross emissions and their warming effect (para 176). Therefore, in light of Articles 3 and 8 of the EIA Directive and the relevant Norwegian implementing legislation, the authorities must carry out an independent assessment of the effects described in the EIA report. Furthermore, the authorities must assess whether conditions should be imposed with a view to limiting and mitigating significant adverse effects (paras 219 ff).
The dissent, penned by Justice Sivertsen, did not challenge the inclusion of downstream combustion emissions within the EIA Directive. Rather, it disputed the majority’s extension of the assessment to cumulative emissions from other existing and approved petroleum projects on the Norwegian continental shelf. For the dissenting justices, an assessment of each project’s gross combustion emissions and their climate effects was sufficient. Accordingly, they found no grounds for invalidating the Ministry’s 2024 decisions (paras 260–264).
The narrow 6–5 majority in the 2026 judgment invites comparison with the Norwegian Supreme Court’s first climate ruling in 2020, when the Court upheld the contested petroleum licences by 11 votes to four. While the outcome differed, there is a striking pattern of judicial continuity.
Seven judges participated in both decisions. Three of the four dissenting judges in 2020 – Webster, Falch and Østensen Berglund – joined the majority in 2026. Conversely, three members of the 2020 majority – Falkanger, Høgetveit Berg and Steinsvik – joined the 2026 dissent. Chief Justice Øie sided with the majority in both cases.
This alignment is particularly interesting because the 2020 dissent was already concerned with the adequacy of EIAs and the need for meaningful judicial scrutiny of procedural requirements. Justice Webster, writing for the minority, argued that judicial restraint in reviewing the substantive environmental choices of the political branches made effective scrutiny of the decision-making procedure all the more important (HR-2020-2472-P, para. 256).
Although the two judgments concern different stages of petroleum authorisation, different legal questions, and an evolving legal framework, the voting patterns suggest a degree of continuity in individual judicial approaches to environmental assessment, institutional deference and the consequences of procedural shortcomings. This observation resonates with Jørn Øyrehagen Sunde’s historical account of the Norwegian Supreme Court. Øyrehagen Sunde connects the Court’s increasingly active role in judicial review with broader institutional developments and internationalisation. In particular, he describes the growing role of legal norms originating beyond Norway’s borders in plenary and Grand Chamber decisions. Viewed through a judicial politics perspective, the 2026 judgment therefore raises a question extending beyond the immediate dispute: How does the internationalisation of law reshape the balance between judicial restraint and effective scrutiny of executive decision-making?
Procedural review, in this sense, is neither procedural formalism nor procedural fetishism. What appears as a procedural turn in climate adjudication may reflect a deeper institutional transformation. The internationalisation of legal norms, instead of allowing courts to “make” climate policy, has empowered their capacity – and responsibility – to scrutinise the legal conditions under which such policy is implemented.
Constitutional Rights and Effective Judicial Review
EIA obligations must be understood in light of Section 112 of the Norwegian Constitution, as recognised in the first Norwegian climate case (HR-2020-2472-P, paras 182–183, as cited in para 221). As the majority writes, “[f]or judicial review to be effective, it is essential that reasons be given”, clearly demonstrating that combustion emissions and their effects on global temperature rise have been taken into account and assessed (para 222).
The royal decree passed by the Norwegian government in May 2026, which reassessed the petroleum approvals, offered a more detailed justification than its 2024 decisions, including an assessment of the emissions’ contribution to climate change. Yet, it still failed to consider the cumulative combustion emissions from existing and approved petroleum fields on the Norwegian continental shelf. Even more importantly, the cumulative climate impacts also should have been addressed in the developers’ environmental impact reports and subjected to public consultation (paras 233–234).
The majority then explains why such an omission invalidates the decisions. Rules on impact assessment for interventions in nature are procedural rules to be enforced strictly, in light of Section 112 of the Constitution and the intensive review it calls for. Their purpose is not only to identify the political trade-offs for the authorities. It is also to give the population knowledge of what planned interventions will do and to secure real public participation in the decision (paras 236–238). The path to invalidity appears therefore short. A decision approving a project within the Directive’s scope that rests on an assessment omitting significant effects meets, by its very nature, the requirement that the error may have affected the outcome (paras 239–240). The democratic rationale for impact assessment is thus written into the remedy.
As the Court explained, the petroleum operators were not parties to the proceedings, and the declaration of invalidity was therefore not binding on them. Consequently, the approvals did not automatically cease to have effect vis-à-vis the licence holders. Rather, the judgment requires the Ministry to reconsider the approvals in accordance with the applicable environmental assessment requirements, potentially confirming, amending or withdrawing them following a legally compliant procedure.
Democracy and the Separation of Powers Principle
Drawing on its 2020 Peoples v Arctic Oil judgment, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that Section 112 of the Norwegian Constitution guarantees environmental rights and access to environmental information. While democratic considerations require judicial restraint in reviewing the political choices underlying environmental decisions, procedural compliance calls for closer scrutiny: the greater a project’s potential consequences, the more rigorous both the environmental assessment and judicial review must be, and the North Sea Fields case concerned procedural errors, rather than the substantive limits of governmental authority (paras 108–111). Writing in the wake of People v Arctic Oil, Minnerop and Røstgaard had already argued that constitutional environmental rights would let courts scrutinise the cumulative effects of global emissions. The Grand Chamber has taken that insight from the field to the shelf.
Who Carries the Risk
The financial stakes are substantial: approximately NOK 21 billion invested in Breidablikk, NOK 7 billion in Tyrving and NOK 177 billion estimated for Yggdrasil (paras 6, 9, 13). Yet the judgment does not decide who would bear the losses if an approval were ultimately revoked. The legal risk was not wholly unforeseeable. US and Australian courts had already addressed combustion emissions (WildEarth Guardians v Zinke and Gloucester Resources v Minister for Planning, both 2019), and Norway’s Supreme Court had indicated in 2020 that global climate effects would be assessed at the PDO stage (paras 4, 7, 10, 155). The Court itself kept the present case alive because it concerned ‘an area under legal development’ of great importance to operators (para 97). Sophisticated licensees could price that risk and arguably should have.
Concluding Remarks
The three Norwegian fields alone are projected to generate close to 400 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent from combustion over their lifetimes (paras 4, 7, 11). This is nine times Norway’s emissions in 2025.
It is worth noting that the global carbon budget will be depleted in less than four years, at current emissions levels, and overshooting 1.5°C is now inevitable. Yet, it remains possible to achieve a ‘lowest possible’ pathway and limit global warming to 1.7–1.8°C before returning to 1.5°C. This allows for a slightly greater budget that future negative emissions may be able to compensate for. EIA can then be considered in relation to scenarios – or their carbon budgets – of the highest possible ambition, the closest to the Paris Agreement objectives.
Just as the ICJ reframed States’ responsibility for climate change in what has been called the Great Reset, the Norwegian Supreme Court’s judgment may mark a reset of its own. The Norwegian reset shows how constitutional procedural rights – as well as interpretation informed by science, regional law and international law – can discipline a (petro-)state’s decisions by amplifying, rather than displacing, democratic choices. Whether more demanding procedure will ultimately change those choices remains open.
